docs.title: Benchmarks
docs.text:
The results on this page come from scripts in the repository and their archived runs, from the paper (TMLR 2026, which describes release 0.4.2), or from the changelog. Results with a random component carry Monte Carlo error from a finite number of trials, so read them at the precision given. Two bugs fixed since the paper change some of its results; they are marked where they apply and described under Corrections since the paper. Installation describes the environment the comparisons need.

Unless a result says otherwise, it was measured with constants inside expressions off (fitted_ops=()), the default before 0.6.0. The scripts build their estimators at the current defaults, so to reproduce an archived result, run the script through the options launcher with the old default:

BEAMFEAT_OPTIONS='{"fitted_ops": []}' \
    python benchmarks/search_stress/with_options.py benchmarks/run_benchmarks.py

This reproduces the archived core-suite R² of every synthetic problem to within 1e-10. At the 0.6.0 defaults, the core suite recovers the same 10/10 formulas, Friedman #1 rises from 0.745 to 0.765 and the other problems move by at most 0.0004; the robustness suite recovers the same 5/5, with R² lower by at most 0.004 (the distractors at 50% noise, 0.776 to 0.772); and the end-to-end calibration below is unchanged.

docs.title: High-dimensional data
docs.text:
benchmarks/additional_experiments/ compares beamfeat with ridge, random forest and LightGBM on the raw columns of nine datasets with 81 to 4,088 columns, over five random 75/25 splits each (the paper's Table 6). Mean held-out R², the best in each row in bold:

dataset columns ridge random forest LightGBM beamfeat formulas tecator 100 0.957 0.717 0.756 0.991 3.6 geomusic 117 0.805 0.739 0.739 0.805 9.6 communities 100 0.650 0.638 0.632 0.641 11.6 riboflavin 4,088 0.579 0.436 0.493 0.544 † 17.4 eyedata 200 0.479 0.340 0.031 0.416 34.0 superconduct 81 0.725 0.884 0.884 0.731 16.2 blogfeedback 280 0.379 0.548 0.535 0.415 18.4 ct_slices 384 0.852 0.981 0.981 0.687 † 14.0 ujiindoorloc 520 0.949 0.995 0.993 0.812 † 20.0

"formulas" is the mean number of terms in beamfeat's fitted equation.

† Corrected since the paper: rerun with 0.5.0, beamfeat's mean R² is 0.340 on riboflavin, 0.664 on ct_slices and 0.816 on ujiindoorloc.

beamfeat leads where the target is a compact algebraic function of a few columns, as on tecator, where ratios of absorbance channels are features that threshold splits cannot build. It trails where the signal is spread thinly over hundreds of columns, as on ct_slices, ujiindoorloc and blogfeedback: ridge keeps every column and shrinks it, while a screen with an error-rate guarantee has little power to reject the null for features that each carry a small fraction of the signal, and leaves them out. With the corrections, it is ahead of both tree ensembles on four of the nine datasets: tecator, geomusic, communities and eyedata. fdr_controlled_ was true on all 90 beamfeat fits of the archived run (the estimator and the transformer).

On tecator, a random forest given the formulas in place of the raw channels goes from 0.739 to 0.992, on three of the five splits. On the small datasets, tree models given the formulas do worse than ridge, which is why ridge is the default.

Tecator also shows what a single fit does not. In the paper's stability study, thirty fits with different seeds on one partition (the design of stability_report(..., resample="seeds")) held R² at 0.989, with a standard deviation of 0.004, while selecting 79 distinct features, counting value-equivalent ones once, none of them in more than 8 of the 30 fits. Adjacent channels correlate at 0.99988, so many band pairs are near-substitutes and each fit picks among them. The user guide shows how to run the same check on other data.

docs.title: Selection calibration
docs.text:
• Selector level (benchmarks/selector_calibration.py). On Gaussian designs over 100 trials, Benjamini–Hochberg realised 0.046 ± 0.008, 0.084 ± 0.012 and 0.161 ± 0.016 at nominal 0.05/0.10/0.20, against its ceiling of q·m₀/m = 0.040/0.080/0.160; Benjamini–Yekutieli, stricter by a harmonic factor, realised 0.013 ± 0.005, 0.018 ± 0.005 and 0.046 ± 0.008. Power was 1.00 throughout. The bounds are computed from the design, and the script stops with an error if a bound falls below a realised rate's whole 95% interval.
  • End to end (benchmarks/calibration_study.py). Search plus holdout selection at nominal FDR 0.10, on 500 rows and 6 input columns of which 2 carry signal through their product, with noise at 5% of the signal's standard deviation: no false discovery in 200 replicates, a 95% upper bound of 0.015 on the true rate, power 1.000 and no fallbacks. Over 60 global-null replicates, nothing was selected.
  • Pure noise (benchmarks/selector_calibration.py). Over 100 global-null pipelines, where every rejection is a false rejection by construction, BH returned features in 6 trials and BY in 1, false discovery proportions of 0.06 and 0.01, both under the nominal 0.10. At this trial count the exact paired test does not reject equal rates (p = 0.06): both corrections saw the same 100 datasets, and the one trial on which BY selected is among BH's six. BY is the estimator default because it is valid under arbitrary dependence, and this result is consistent with that choice.

The guarantees page states what each procedure guarantees and under which assumptions.

docs.title: Formula recovery
docs.text:
• Known formulas (benchmarks/run_benchmarks.py, 70/30 splits). Mean R² over the ten core-suite problems, and recovery of the generating columns over the ten synthetic problems that declare them; the two sets differ by one dataset each. beamfeat: mean R² 0.9989, fits of about 0.2 s, 10/10 recovered. autofeat: 0.9970, about 12 s, 8/10. LightGBM 0.9798, ridge 0.8442. On the purely linear problem, where feature construction has nothing to add, ridge ties beamfeat.
  • Feynman equations (benchmarks/feynman_panel.py, 12 physics laws, 0.1% noise). 10/12 solved at the SRBench criterion, and the exact symbolic form on 8 of the 9 laws that have one, at 0.9 s per equation in the archived run, which predates the 0.5.0 search speed-up. The misses there are known limits of the search space: a depth-3 rational, a literal constant, depth-4 nesting and the Gaussian's exponential. With fitted_ops, on by default since 0.6.0, the last two are within reach: the Gaussian comes out as exp(-0.5*(x0)^2) and relativistic velocity addition as (x0 + x1)/((x0*x1) + 1), the exact form on 10 of the 11 laws that have one within the depth, still 10/12 solved, at 0.4 s per equation.
  • Heavy-tailed noise (Student t(2), infinite variance). The exact formula is recovered, at R² 0.956 against LightGBM's 0.866. The permutation test is distribution-free, so heavy tails do not affect its validity.

docs.title: Distractors and false features
docs.text:
Signal hidden among ten distractor columns. A false feature is a returned formula touching only irrelevant ones; the count is over the five stress datasets that declare which columns their formula uses. Regenerate with python benchmarks/make_figures.py, which writes six other figures alongside it.

  • Stress suite (signal among ten distractor columns). beamfeat's false-feature rate, the share of returned formulas that touch only irrelevant columns, is 0.000 at noise levels from 5% to 50% of the signal scale and at n as small as 120, with recovery and the guarantee intact throughout. autofeat recovers the formula as often but returns distractor-only features on 2 of the 5 scoreable datasets. The comparison is a count rather than a mean, since a mean over five datasets carries a standard error of about 0.15, and autofeat's output varies between processes.
  • OpenFE on the same suite (its features feeding LightGBM, after shimming a removed scikit-learn parameter): a false-feature rate of 0.000 as well, but 0/5 formulas recovered and a lower R² on all five. It optimises a tree model's lift rather than equations.
  • Selection alone (knockpy on the raw columns, with the modified-FDR offset, the only satisfiable configuration at these dimensionalities): 0/15 formulas recovered, a core-suite R² at the ridge level (0.845), and distractor-only features on 2 of the 5 scoreable stress datasets. The difference from beamfeat is the construction step and the holdout.

docs.title: Real datasets
docs.text: Seven datasets, numeric columns only. beamfeat leads on mpg (0.864 against LightGBM's 0.853) and on tips, where gradient boosting overfits below ridge while the FDR screen keeps beamfeat at the top. It ties ridge on diamonds with one interpretable feature. It trails LightGBM on penguins, breast cancer and California housing (0.700 against 0.843, where the signal is spatial), and ridge on diabetes (0.376), where there is no nonlinear structure to find and beamfeat adds none.

docs.title: Known limits
docs.text:
• Piecewise targets suit trees: on a threshold problem, LightGBM reaches 0.998 and beamfeat 0.808. When a tree model beats beamfeat by a wide margin, the signal is likely piecewise rather than algebraic. OpenFE also records 0.998 there, but bit-identically to raw LightGBM and from a feature touching only an irrelevant column, so the result belongs to its tree model.
  • Laws whose parts do not correlate with the target (benchmarks/search_stress/). With centred inputs, the parts of x0*x1*x2, and of x0*x1 among hundreds of columns, do not correlate with the target, so the default search can drop them before it combines them. Over 50 fits per cell, on inputs uniform on (-1, 1), x0*x1*x2 is recovered exactly in every fit with 5 columns but in 0.54, 0.18 and 0.10 of them with 20, 100 and 300, and x0*x1 in 0.32 with 1,000 columns; on shifted inputs the same laws are recovered in every fit. A wider beam does not close the gap. The opt-in magnitude_slots=10 recovered every lost cell but one crowded sum law (0.88), at 1.2 to 1.7 times the fit time, and left the real-data suites and the false-discovery rates essentially unchanged; the guide shows how to use it.
  • Friedman #1 (benchmarks/friedman_decomposition.py). Over six draws, a representation oracle reaches 0.960 ± 0.003, a screening-admissible ceiling 0.874 ± 0.006, and the pipeline 0.780 ± 0.013. About 0.086 is lost to what marginal screening cannot see: the centred quadratic term is nearly uncorrelated with the target on its own, so a marginal screen has almost no power to reject its null. The other 0.094 is lost in the search. The guarantees page explains the marginal null.

docs.title: Independent comparison
docs.text:
benchmarks/independent/ holds a 360-fit study (nine datasets, eight methods, five splits, average ranks and a Friedman test) with its harness, pinned environment, data, and a notebook that reproduces the analysis. Mean held-out R²: random forest 0.810, beamfeat 0.803, LightGBM 0.798, OpenFE 0.736, ridge 0.704, autofeat −1.561 and featuretools −2.478. The worst of each method's 45 fits: beamfeat 0.355, autofeat −103.2 and featuretools −57.3; no beamfeat fit fell below zero. beamfeat ran at about 60 times autofeat's speed, and fdr_controlled_ was true on 45 of 45 fits. The featuretools figures come from a harness that filled its non-finite test cells with 0; with the training medians, as the harness now fills them, they read 0.461 and −12.882 (see Corrections since the paper).

PROVENANCE.md records what reproduces and what does not. beamfeat's selections reproduce bit-identically, though the fitted model's cross-validated penalty can flip on marginal problems. autofeat sets no random_state and draws its decoy features from the global NumPy generator: six runs on one identical split ranged from +0.952 to −109.8.

docs.title: Relationship to autofeat
docs.text: beamfeat's design began from a code review of autofeat (Horn et al., 2019). It keeps autofeat's central idea, compact symbolic features feeding a linear model, and replaces exhaustive expansion with beam search, noise-threshold selection with FDR-controlled procedures, and upper-pinned dependencies with tested floors. The generate-then-filter design has a direct precedent in tsfresh (Christ et al., 2018), which filters mass-generated time-series features under Benjamini–Yekutieli control; beamfeat applies it to symbolic expressions on tabular columns. Migrating from autofeat maps one API onto the other.

docs.title: Test suite
docs.text: 965 tests at 97% statement coverage, with a 90% floor enforced in CI, including scikit-learn's full estimator-conformance checks.

docs.title: Corrections since the paper
docs.text:
The paper describes release 0.4.2, archived with its run records at 10.5281/zenodo.23417132. Two bugs, fixed in 0.5.0, change results it reports. The archived records are kept as they were run.

  • Comparison harness. The harness filled non-finite test cells of the constructed features with 0, while the training cells got the training median. This understated featuretools, whose ratio features divide by columns that contain zeros. With the training medians on both, featuretools has a mean R² of about 0.461 rather than −2.478 in the independent comparison, a worst fit of −12.882 rather than −57.320, and one fit below zero rather than six. Every other method's row, and every conclusion about beamfeat, is unaffected (PROVENANCE.md).
  • Search. When max_candidates_per_depth bound at depth 1, the first round proposed parents in column order, so from about 258 inputs, pairs among the last columns were never proposed. The first round now proposes the inputs in order of their score, as documented. Three datasets of the high-dimensional study reach the ceiling. Rerun with 0.5.0, beamfeat's mean R² is 0.340 on riboflavin, 0.664 on ct_slices and 0.816 on ujiindoorloc, against 0.544, 0.687 and 0.812 in the paper; the archived riboflavin run was made with an earlier version, and 0.4.4 gives 0.523 there. With the ceiling raised so that every input is proposed, ct_slices and ujiindoorloc give the new results exactly; the old ones depended on which columns came first in the file. beamfeat now leads both tree ensembles on four of the nine datasets rather than five.

Later releases are also faster, so the paper's timings and memory figures describe 0.4.2. 0.5.0 runs the high-dimensional study 2 to 28 times faster per dataset without changing any feature, p-value or prediction, and a default fit on 1000 columns and 600 rows that peaked at 2.6 GB of memory now peaks at 0.35 GB. The changelog lists every change.

docs.title: Statistical guarantees
docs.text: This page states, for each selection procedure, exactly what is guaranteed, under which assumptions, and what was measured. Every number here is reproduced by the committed test suite (tests/test_selection.py, tests/test_estimators.py) or benchmark scripts. Calibration figures come from 100 trials and are quoted with their standard error; read them at that precision rather than at the last digit.

docs.title: What "FDR control at level q" means
docs.text:
Each candidate j carries its own null hypothesis H₀ⱼ. For the default screen, H₀ⱼ is that candidate j is independent of the target. A selection procedure rejects some of these nulls, and the candidates whose nulls it rejects are its discoveries: the selected features, which beamfeat also calls the screened or certified set. Rejecting a true null is a false discovery, a Type I error. With R rejections of which V are false, the false discovery proportion is FDP = V / max(R, 1), and the false discovery rate is its expectation over repetitions of the experiment, FDR = E[FDP]. A single run with FDP above q is consistent with control; a mean over trials above q is not. All documentation and tests in beamfeat use this definition.

Under the global null, where every H₀ⱼ is true, V = R, so the FDR is the probability of rejecting any null at all. Controlling it at q then means that at most a fraction q of pure-noise fits select anything.

docs.title: Permutation selector (default)
docs.text:
Statistic. |Pearson correlation| (regression) or eta-squared (classification) between each candidate and the target — a fixed function of the data, which is the condition for a permutation test to be valid. Statistics that re-tune themselves on the observed target (e.g. a cross-validated lasso penalty) violate exchangeability unless the tuning is repeated inside every permutation; beamfeat deliberately avoids them.

P-values. Add-one estimator (1 + #exceedances)/(B + 1) (Phipson & Smyth, 2010): valid in finite samples, and never zero. The floor 1/(B+1) interacts with the multiplicity correction — Benjamini–Hochberg needs the leading feature to reach q/m, Benjamini–Yekutieli the smaller q/(m c(m)) — so B is auto-raised to twice the bound belonging to the configured correction (satisfiability plus headroom for one null exceedance), capped at max_permutations. The requirement binds hardest when few candidates reach the floor together: several tied signals relax the threshold by their count, a lone one carries it alone. If the pool is large enough that even the cap cannot meet it, the selector says so in warnings_raised and an empty selection should be read as an exhausted budget rather than an absent signal.

Null semantics. Marginal independence: H₀ⱼ is that candidate j is independent of the target. A near-duplicate of a genuine signal is not independent of the target, so rejecting its null is a true discovery; de-duplication is performed by the search's redundancy threshold, not the error-control procedure.

Multiplicity. The estimators (BeamFeatRegressor, BeamFeatClassifier, BeamFeatTransformer) default to Benjamini–Yekutieli, valid under arbitrary dependence; PermutationSelector used directly defaults to Benjamini–Hochberg, valid under positive regression dependence (PRDS). Engineered candidates share parents and are mutually correlated by construction, so PRDS cannot be taken for granted and the estimators take the conservative option. Over 100 pure-noise pipelines BH returned features in 6 trials against BY's 1 (FDP 0.06 and 0.01, benchmarks/selector_calibration.py), both under the nominal 0.10. At this trial count the exact paired test does not reject equal rates (p = 0.06): both corrections saw the same 100 datasets, and the one trial on which BY selected is among BH's six. Read it as a consistency check rather than as evidence that BH loses control here. A selector instance passed to an estimator keeps its own settings, so selector=PermutationSelector() runs BH at the instance's target_fdr; the estimator warns when its selection_correction or target_fdr disagrees with the instance's.

Measured calibration (Gaussian designs, 300 rows, 25 candidates, 5 signals, 100 trials). BH controls the FDR at q·m0/m, here q·20/25, and realised 0.046 ± 0.008, 0.084 ± 0.012 and 0.161 ± 0.016 at nominal 0.05/0.10/0.20 against ceilings of 0.040/0.080/0.160. BY is stricter by a harmonic factor and realised 0.013 ± 0.005, 0.018 ± 0.005 and 0.046 ± 0.008. Power 1.00 throughout. benchmarks/selector_calibration.py derives each bound from the design and stops with an error if a bound falls below a realised rate's whole 95% interval, so these figures cannot drift from the behaviour.

What the marginal null cannot see. A feature can be jointly essential yet nearly marginally independent of the target — a centred quadratic (c − 0.5)² contributes almost no marginal correlation until its linear complement is fitted. The marginal screen has almost no power to reject the null for such a feature, and where the feature is exactly marginally independent of the target, failing to reject is correct under that null. The cost is measurable on targets built from them (Friedman #1, over six draws: the screen never rejects the null for c, giving a screening-admissible ceiling of 0.874 ± 0.006 against a representation oracle of 0.960 ± 0.003, with the pipeline reaching 0.780 ± 0.013. Around 0.086 is lost to screening and 0.094 to the search. The null for c² is rejected on some draws and not others, since (c − 0.5)² expands to carry a little marginal signal through it.) Joint selection recovers such features but certifies nothing; that trade is the design.

docs.title: Knockoff selector
docs.text:
Fixed-X (Barber & Candès, 2015), used when n > 2p: no distributional assumption on the features — deterministic engineered columns are fine. The guarantee requires the linear model with Gaussian, homoskedastic noise. The construction's exchangeability identities X̃'X̃ = X'X and X'X̃ = X'X − sI are verified to numerical precision by the tests, also after the centring the lasso statistic applies (the knockoffs are built orthogonal to the intercept as well, which takes one row more than 2p). On a near-singular design (smallest covariance eigenvalue below 1e-6) valid knockoffs of the dependent columns would equal the originals, and the lasso's tie-breaking would then favour the originals; constant and linearly dependent columns are therefore left out of the construction, get W = 0, and are named in a runtime warning. Routing and the n > 2p requirement count the retained columns.

Statistic. The fixed-X guarantee holds for a statistic that sees the data only through [X X̃]'[X X̃] and [X X̃]'y. On the fixed-X path for regression beamfeat uses the lasso-path signed maximum, W_j = max(Z_j, Z̃_j)·sign(Z_j − Z̃_j), where Z_j is the penalty at which column j enters the path, computed from those inner products alone; a test checks that rotating the rows, which preserves them, leaves W unchanged. Versions up to 0.5.0 used the difference of cross-validated lasso coefficients there, whose folds look at individual rows, so the guarantee did not strictly cover it. On Gaussian linear models at q = 0.2 (200 trials each) knockoff+ realised 0.180, 0.172 and 0.135 with the path statistic against 0.151, 0.165 and 0.155 before, with power 0.96, 0.98 and 0.48 against 0.97, 0.99 and 0.82: both under the level, and the price of the valid statistic is power when columns are correlated (0.7 between neighbours in the third design). Model-X, which admits any statistic that swaps sign with the pair, keeps the cross-validated one.

Model-X Gaussian (Candès et al., 2018), used only when n ≤ 2p: assumes jointly Gaussian features, which engineered features violate; a warning is recorded, and the permutation selector is recommended in this regime.

The estimators surface every selector diagnostic — assumption strain, unsatisfiable configurations — through the warnings module, so an empty knockoff result reads as "could not have selected at this configuration" rather than "no evidence"; when knockoff+ selects nothing but offset=0 would have, the warning says so and names the trade-off.

Offsets. offset=1 (knockoff+) carries the finite-sample FDR guarantee and realised 0.170 at nominal 0.20 over 100 trials; it is unsatisfiable with fewer than 1/q features, and a warning fires on narrow designs. offset=0 controls only a modified FDR and realised 0.260, above offset=1 as expected. (With the cross-validated statistic used until 0.5.0, 0.159 and 0.249.) Both move across numeric stacks, since knockoff construction depends on matrix decompositions; treat the ordering and the nominal bound as the claim, not the second decimal. benchmarks/selector_calibration.py regenerates both, and the committed tests pin the ordering rather than the decimals.

docs.title: Selective inference: why the estimators split their data
docs.text:
The search retains candidates because they correlate with the target in its sample. P-values computed on that same sample are therefore optimistically biased, and the nominal FDR is not guaranteed for them. By default the estimators search on one half of the training rows and run selection on the other (selection_holdout=0.5), restoring the fixed-candidate-set premise. Measured end-to-end over 200 replicates at nominal 0.10 (500 rows, 6 input columns of which 2 carry signal through their product, noise at 5% of the signal's standard deviation, max_depth=2, beam_width=25): not one false discovery, a 95% upper bound of 0.015 on the true rate, power 1.000, no fallbacks; 60 global-null replicates selected nothing. That is a far stronger signal than the selector-level design above — the generating feature correlates with the target at 0.999 — so read it as an end-to-end check that the split does its job, not as a power measurement at the margin. benchmarks/calibration_study.py regenerates it. If the holdout is disabled, the estimator refuses to claim the guarantee (fdr_controlled_ = False).

Constants fitted inside expressions (fitted_ops) are part of the search. Each is chosen inside the search, on the search rows, before selection sees the candidates, and the selection rows receive every expression with its constant fixed, as they receive its structure. The fixed-candidate-set premise therefore holds as before and the guarantee is unchanged. A fitted constant is one more way the search adapts to its sample, so with selection_holdout=None, where search and screen share rows, it adds to the optimism for which the estimator already declines the claim. On pure-noise targets (50 seeds, 200 rows, 5 columns, defaults otherwise) the fraction of fits with any discovery was the same with all four fitted operators as without: 0/50 for regression, 2/50 for classification. The four are on by default since 0.6.0; at that default the end-to-end study above gives the same result as without them (no false discovery in 200 replicates, power 1.000, nothing selected in 60 global-null replicates), as does the pure-noise pipeline stress (BH 6/100, BY 1/100).

magnitude_slots changes which expressions the search keeps, not how they are tested. Its magnitude score is computed inside the search, on the search rows, as the score is; the expressions it keeps are built on and ranked like any other; and the selection rows receive the search's output as a fixed set of expressions, chosen without them. The premise of the screen holds as before and its guarantee is unchanged. Measured on 200 paired replicates per design at q = 0.1 (benchmarks/search_stress/null.py, the screened set), the share of fits with at least one false discovery was the same with the option as without on four null designs, 0.015 to 0.025, among them centred and Gaussian inputs and 200 columns on 150 search rows; on a planted x0*x1*x2 among centred distractors it was 0.025 against 0.020, one fit in 200, with a false discovery rate of 0.005 either way.

docs.title: Columns inside a term (input_test)
docs.text:
The screen's null is that a term is independent of the target, so (x0*x1)/(x1 + x8) is a true discovery when y = x0*x1: x0*x1 carries it, however unrelated x8 is. A reader of the equation still takes x8 to matter. input_test=True tests each column inside each candidate that reads more than one: the column's rows are permuted, wherever it occurs in the expression, and the screen's statistic is recomputed. The null for a column is that it is independent of the target and of the candidate's other columns together; under it, with independent rows from one distribution, permuting the column leaves the distribution of the data unchanged, so the p-values are exact. The screen's step-up correction runs across every (candidate, column) pair of every candidate, so which pairs are tested does not depend on the screen's outcome. A screened term is dropped before parsimony when the test fails to reject the null for any of its columns; input_report_ lists every pair, with null_rejected marking the pairs whose null the test rejected.

What it does not cover: a junk column correlated with a real one is not null in this sense, so its null can be rejected and the term kept. Testing it given the other columns needs a model of the column given the others (knockoffs or the conditional randomisation test), which this test does not assume. The screen's guarantee is unchanged and still covers the screened set.

Measured on 20 seeds of y = x0*x1 plus 25% noise among 10 junk columns (500 training and 500 test rows), against the default: printed equations with a junk column 14 → 1, printed terms with one 23/45 → 1/28, held-out R² 0.9413 → 0.9416. With the junk x8 correlated 0.82 with x1, 10 → 3. On pure-noise targets the screen rejects no null with the option or without it, and the physics panel is unchanged.

docs.title: Parsimony within the screened set
docs.text:
Three things can be wanted of the fitted equation: that it be short, that the guarantee cover the terms actually printed, and that it cost no selection rows. Any two are available together, and the choice is one parameter.

parsimony="forward" (the default) applies greedy forward selection within the screened set and fits the compact subset. It is short and costs no rows. What it gives up is the second property: the subset is chosen on the rows selection already used, so the q-level guarantee certifies the set it was drawn from and not the terms the forward step retained. equation() says so on its own output whenever terms were dropped —

y = 0.9999*(x0 * x1) - 0.003943   [1 of 25 certified terms; parsimony=None prints all 25]

— and fdr_scope_ records the same thing for code, which never sees that string: "screened set" here, "printed equation" when the guarantee covers the returned features themselves. fdr_controlled_ says whether there is a guarantee; fdr_scope_ says what it is over. The full screened set with exact p- and q-values per candidate stays auditable in selection_report_. fdp_inflation_ reports |S|/|S'|, the factor by which pruning can inflate the realised false discovery proportion: the denominator shrinks faster than the numerator, so the count of false discoveries cannot rise but the proportion can.

parsimony=None prints the screened set entire. The guarantee covers what is printed — the equation is the certified object, not a selection from it — and it still costs no rows. The price is length: on wide data the equation runs to dozens of terms. fdp_inflation_ is 1.0, because the printed set and the screened set are the same set.

parsimony_holdout buys both, and pays in rows. It splits the selection rows again: screening and parsimony use the first part, and the resulting subset — fixed at that point, and so an ordinary fixed-candidate set — is re-tested on the part held back. Terms whose null the re-test fails to reject are dropped, and because the guarantee then does cover the printed terms, equation() prints no subset note. The cost is real: comfortable above a few hundred rows, unaffordable below roughly a hundred, where parsimony=None is the better choice. If a compact certified equation cannot be produced, the whole screened set is returned rather than a pruned subset — the pruned subset is the one thing a caller asking for certification did not want.

Measured. benchmarks/parsimony_holdout/ calibrates the procedure over 48,000 fits: a global null, and y = a*b/c plus noise among 5 or 20 distractors, with and without a column correlated 0.9 with a, at signal-to-noise ratios 1 and 3 and with 300 and 1,000 rows, 200 replicates per cell, at q = 0.1 and 0.2, beside the default and parsimony=None on the same data. The figures below are means over replicates. Their Monte Carlo standard errors are in the study's report, and are at most 0.012 for a design pooled over its four cells.

  • In the marginal sense, the guarantee's, the printed equation's realised FDR stayed far below q under every setting. On the global null it was 0.009 to 0.018 at q = 0.1 and 0.021 to 0.029 at q = 0.2 (a term printed in 7 to 14 and 17 to 23 fits of 800), and on the planted and proxy designs no setting printed a term built only from distractors in 3,200 fits per level. The re-test added nothing measurable here. On null data it failed to reject the null for the screen's rare false discoveries, in 20 of 22 fits at q = 0.1, and the fallback to the screened set then printed them anyway, so the printed equation's error is the screen's own.
  • In the conditional sense, counting a printed term that uses any column outside the generating formula, such as a rider (a*b/c) * x7, no setting controls the rate and the marginal re-test does not lower it. It was 0.67 to 0.77 under every setting at a signal-to-noise ratio of 1, where the forward step retains 18 terms on average. At a ratio of 3 it was 0.42 to 0.44 at the default and 0.53 to 0.62 with the re-test: on its smaller share of rows the forward step retains more riders, and each rider is associated with the target, so the re-test rejects its null.
  • Power to print the generating term (0.85 to 0.93 at a ratio of 1, 0.99 to 1.00 at 3) and held-out R² (within 0.0033 of the default, paired) hardly moved under any setting.

certify_test="conditional" re-tests each frozen term given the others rather than on its own, with a Freedman–Lane permutation test (Freedman & Lane, 1983): the target and the term are residualised on the other terms and an intercept, the target's residuals are permuted, the statistic is the partial correlation, and the screen's step-up correction is applied at the screen's level. The null for a term is that its coefficient is zero in the linear model of the target on all the frozen terms: given the others, it adds nothing linear. That null is relative to the frozen set, so a term standing in for a true one the set leaves out is not null under it, and rejecting its null is not a false rejection. The p-values are approximate. For a single term the test is the marginal permutation test and exact. With others present its validity rests on the errors of a linear model of the target on the other terms being exchangeable (independent and identically distributed, so of constant variance), and even then the residuals it permutes are estimated and only nearly exchangeable, so the p-values are close to exact rather than exact (Anderson & Robinson, 2001; Winkler et al., 2014). The test is for regression only, and the step-up correction inherits its own condition: Benjamini–Yekutieli holds under any dependence among the p-values, Benjamini–Hochberg needs positive dependence.

Measured in the same study, at a signal-to-noise ratio of 3 it brought the conditional rate to 0.18 to 0.22, paired −0.21 to −0.26 against the default. In the fits where it rejected at least one null it printed 1.1 to 1.2 terms, with a conditional rate of 0.026 to 0.040 at q = 0.1 and 0.052 to 0.073 at q = 0.2, and power 0.98 to 0.99. Its weakness is the fallback. When the frozen subset is long and its terms nearly reproduce one another, no term adds anything given the rest, the test rejects no null, and the screened set is returned, which carries the screen's marginal guarantee only. That happened in 87 to 92% of fits at a ratio of 1 and in 18 to 26% at 3 (37 to 52% with 300 rows, under 1% with 1,000). certification_result_.n_selected is 0 on such a fit.

The equation list. equations() and equations_ record the forward path through the whole screened set, one equation per number of terms, at every setting above. Each line is a subset of the screened set chosen on the rows screening used, the same kind of selection as the default fitted equation, so the guarantee covers none of them but the last, which is the screened set itself, and, under parsimony_holdout, the re-tested fitted equation. An equation picked from the list after reading it is not covered; the list says so in its last line.

docs.title: What the default costs
docs.text:
The exchange above is stated rather than assumed elsewhere in this page, so it is measured here. benchmarks/parsimony_cost.py re-runs the affected studies at both settings and pairs them fit by fit; benchmarks/PARSIMONY_COST.md records which studies depend on the setting and why. Over 308 paired fits across four studies:

study fits mean ΔR² (forward − None) worst ΔR² terms, None ÷ forward fdr_controlled_ disagreements end-to-end calibration 260 −0.0001 −0.0003 25.0× 0 known-formula + stress suites 18 −0.0008 −0.0148 26.0× 0 Feynman physics panel 24 −0.0009 −0.0111 30.6× 0 Friedman #1 decomposition 6 −0.0095 −0.0192 3.6× 0

Compactness costs about a thousandth of R² on average and at most 0.019 on a single fit, and buys an equation roughly twenty-five times shorter. R² is held out in every study but the end-to-end calibration, which fits and scores on the same rows. fdr_controlled_ never disagreed between the two settings on any of the 308 fits, and the end-to-end calibration figures above — empirical FDR, its upper bound, power, fallbacks, null selections — are identical at both settings to every digit reported.

Pruning was also never observed to inflate the realised false discovery proportion. That is not a theorem and should not be read as one: |S|/|S'| is the only bound available, and it is weak. It is an empirical observation with a mechanism behind it — greedy forward selection ranks by predictive contribution, and a marginally null feature contributes nothing, so it tends to be dropped first rather than kept. On a selector-level stress where screening was made to reject many true nulls (Gaussian design, nominal q = 0.5, 300 trials), the screened set realised FDP 0.397 and the greedily pruned subset realised 0.000, with the proportion rising in none of the 300 trials.

docs.title: Association is not generalisation
docs.text: FDR screening bounds the expected share of selected features that are not associated with the target. It does not certify that the linear model assembled from them generalises: a true discovery can carry extreme leverage — a reciprocal or logarithm evaluated near its pole — that destabilises the least-squares fit at points close to the singularity. The estimators keep these claims separate with a post-fit check on the selection holdout: a negative held-out R² (regression) or held-out accuracy below the majority-class rate (classification) raises a visible DegenerateFitWarning naming the gap. Rank-based scoring deserves particular attention here, since rank transformation hides exactly the magnitudes that cause the problem.

docs.title: When no null is rejected
docs.text: When the screen rejects no null, the default (on_no_discoveries="empty") uses no constructed features: the model degrades to an intercept-only fit (training mean, or class prior for classification), fdr_controlled_ is False, and a visible NoDiscoveriesWarning is raised. "fallback" uses the unfiltered search output, also with fdr_controlled_ = False; "raise" raises. In every mode, check fdr_controlled_ before treating fitted features as statistically vetted.

docs.title: User guide
docs.text: Everything below is runnable as-is; outputs shown are from real runs.

docs.title: Sixty seconds to a vetted equation
docs.text:
import numpy as np
from beamfeat import BeamFeatRegressor

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
X = rng.uniform(1, 6, (400, 4))
y = X[:, 0] * X[:, 1] + rng.normal(0, 0.05, 400)

model = BeamFeatRegressor(max_depth=2, beam_width=25, random_state=0).fit(X, y)
print(model.equation())
print(model.fdr_controlled_)

y = 0.9999*(x0 * x1) - 0.003943   [1 of 25 certified terms; parsimony=None prints all 25]
True

Three things matter. equation() is the fitted model itself — evaluate it on raw feature values and you reproduce predict(). fdr_controlled_ states whether the features carry the false-discovery-rate guarantee; check it before treating them as statistically vetted. And the suffix says that those two do not describe the same set of terms.

That last point has an attribute as well as a suffix, because a script never reads the printed string:

print(model.fdr_controlled_, "|", model.fdr_scope_)

True | screened set

fdr_controlled_ says whether there is a guarantee. fdr_scope_ says what it is over: "screened set" when the printed terms were pruned from a larger certified set, "printed equation" when the guarantee covers the terms you are looking at, None when there is no guarantee to scope. Branch on fdr_scope_, not on the equation text.

docs.title: Why the equation says "1 of 25"
docs.text:
The screen rejected the null for twenty-five formulas, the certified set. Each formula's null is that it is independent of the target, and on a strong signal every near-duplicate of the true feature really is associated with the target, so rejecting its null is correct and twenty-five is the honest size of the certified set. A parsimony step then selects the compact predictive subset and fits that, because an equation of dozens of near-duplicate terms defeats the interpretability the library exists for.

The subset is chosen on the rows selection already used, so the q-level guarantee covers the twenty-five it came from and not the one the forward step retained. That is what the suffix records, and fdp_inflation_ prices it:

print(model.fdp_inflation_)

25.0

|S|/|S'|, the factor by which pruning can inflate the realised false discovery proportion, since the denominator shrinks faster than the numerator can. Set parsimony=None to fit the screened set entire, at which point the printed equation is the certified object and the suffix disappears:

full = BeamFeatRegressor(max_depth=2, beam_width=25, random_state=0,
                         parsimony=None).fit(X, y)
print(full.n_features_out_)
print(full.equation(max_terms=3))

25
y = 1.077*(x0 * x1) - 0.2264*(x0 * sqrt(x1)) - 0.5879*(sqrt(x1) - 1/(x0)) + 1.369

max_terms shortens the display, not the model: the terms it leaves out are held at their training mean, and their average contribution moves into the constant, which is why it differs from the full equation's.

What the default costs you in fit is small, and measured rather than asserted: about a thousandth of R² across 308 paired fits (held out in every study but the end-to-end calibration, which scores in-sample), for an equation some twenty-five times shorter, with no case where pruning inflated the realised false discovery proportion. The measurement is benchmarks/PARSIMONY_COST.md. Short and certified costs rows instead of the guarantee: see parsimony_holdout on the guarantees page, and the next section.

docs.title: Re-testing the printed terms
docs.text:
parsimony_holdout holds back that fraction of the selection rows. Screening and the forward step run on the rest, and the terms they return, fixed at that point, are tested again on the rows held back; terms whose null the re-test fails to reject are dropped. By default the re-test is the screen again (certify_test="marginal"), which tests each term's association with the target on its own. It rejects the null for a term that only rides on a true one, since such a term is associated with the target through the true one. certify_test="conditional" tests each term given the other printed terms instead:

import numpy as np
from beamfeat import BeamFeatRegressor

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
X = rng.uniform(0.5, 3.0, (600, 8))
y = 2 * X[:, 0] + rng.normal(0, 0.5, 600)  # x0 alone

# Products only, and the whole screened set: every product of x0 with
# another column rides on x0, and the re-test sees them all.
options = dict(max_depth=1, binary_ops=("mul",), unary_ops=(), parsimony=None,
               parsimony_holdout=0.5, random_state=0)
marginal = BeamFeatRegressor(**options).fit(X, y)
conditional = BeamFeatRegressor(**options, certify_test="conditional").fit(X, y)
print(marginal.formulas())
print(conditional.equation())

['x0', '(x0 * x7)', '(x0 * x6)', '(x0 * x3)', '(x0 * x2)', '(x0 * x1)', '(x0 * x5)', '(x0 * x4)']
y = 2.009*x0 - 0.003251

The conditional re-test is a permutation test for regression only, and its p-values are approximate; the guarantees page states its null and what its validity rests on. It works when the subset it receives is short. When the subset is long and its terms nearly reproduce one another, no term adds anything given the rest, the re-test rejects no null, and the estimator returns the whole screened set, which carries only the screen's marginal guarantee; certification_result_.n_selected is then 0, and a NoDiscoveriesWarning says so. In the calibration study (benchmarks/parsimony_holdout/) that happened in about nine fits in ten at a signal-to-noise ratio of 1, where the forward step retains 18 terms on average, and in about one in five at a ratio of 3. At that ratio, the share of printed terms using a column outside the generating formula was 0.42 to 0.44 at the defaults, 0.53 to 0.62 with the marginal re-test and 0.18 to 0.22 with the conditional one, which printed about one term in the fits it did not hand back to the screened set. Both re-tests cost rows: hold back a fraction only when the selection rows number a few hundred or more.

docs.title: Columns that ride along inside a term
docs.text:
The screen tests each term as a whole, so a term that attaches a junk column to the true one is still a true discovery: ((x0 * x1) / (x0 + x6)) is associated with the target through x0 * x1, however unrelated x6 is. input_test=True tests each column inside each term that reads more than one. The column's rows are permuted wherever it occurs in the expression, and its null is that it is independent of the target and of the term's other columns. A screened term is dropped before the forward step when the test fails to reject the null for any of its columns:

import numpy as np
from beamfeat import BeamFeatRegressor

rng = np.random.default_rng(11)
X = rng.uniform(1, 6, (500, 12))
signal = X[:, 0] * X[:, 1]
y = signal + rng.normal(0, 0.25 * np.std(signal), 500)
print(BeamFeatRegressor(random_state=0).fit(X, y).equation())
print(BeamFeatRegressor(random_state=0, input_test=True).fit(X, y).equation())

y = 1.052*(x0 * x1) - 0.4088*((x0 * x1) / (x0 + x6)) - 0.1452*((x3 / x0) - x1) + 0.1295*((x5 / x0) - x1) + 0.04642   [4 of 50 certified terms; parsimony=None prints all 50]
y = 1.013*(x0 * x1) - 0.1608   [1 of 50 certified terms; parsimony=None prints all 8; input_test dropped 42]

input_report_ lists every (term, column) pair with its p- and q-value, and null_rejected marks the pairs whose null the test rejected. The screen's guarantee is unchanged and still covers the screened set of 50. A junk column that is correlated with a real one is not null in this sense, so its null can be rejected and the term kept; the guarantees page states what the test covers and what was measured. It is opt-in because it costs time that grows with the rows: here the fit took about seven times as long, and n_jobs threads share the tests.

docs.title: The equation at every size
docs.text:
The forward step adds terms one at a time and stops when the next adds less than parsimony_tol to R². equations() shows the step continued through the whole screened set, one equation per number of terms, so you can see what the stopping point traded away:

print(model.equations(max_n_terms=3))

Forward path through the 25 screened terms. R^2 is in-sample, on the rows screening used; gain is the R^2 the line's last term adds.
  k complexity    R^2      gain equation
* 1          4 0.9999    0.9999 y ~ (x0 * x1)
  2         10 0.9999 1.159e-06 y ~ (x0 * x1) + ((x0 + x3) * x1)
  3         18 0.9999 1.103e-06 y ~ (x0 * x1) + ((x0 + x3) * x1) + ((x0 * x1) * (x1 * x2))
  ...
* the fitted model (the forward step stops before the first gain below parsimony_tol=0.001).
The FDR guarantee covers the screened set of 25 terms (line 25), not an equation chosen from this list.

Complexity counts the nodes in each term's expression tree — operators and input columns, (x0 * x1) being 3 — plus one per term for its coefficient and one per fitted constant. The lines are written y ~ a + b, without coefficients, because only the marked one has been fitted; equation() prints its coefficients. For a classifier the R² is that of the integer-coded labels, the heuristic the forward step ranks by, not a classification metric.

The last line of the output is the one to keep in mind. Every line is a subset of the screened set chosen on the rows screening used, so picking line 3 because it looks better is the same kind of choice the forward step makes, and the guarantee covers it no more than it covers the fitted line. Recording the path changes nothing that is fitted, and it is recorded at parsimony=None as well, where the marked line is the last.

The records behind the text are in equations_, one dict per line with n_terms, complexity, r2, formulas, the features as expression nodes, and model, which marks the fitted line. It is None without a selector and empty when the screen rejected no null.

docs.title: One equation or one of many
docs.text:
A fit prints one equation, found on one random split of the training rows into the part the search sees and the part selection tests on. Where many expressions predict about equally well, another split prints another equation, and nothing in a single fit says which case you are in. stability_report finds out. It refits clones of the estimator on random splits of the data, scores each once on a test part its fit never saw, and counts the distinct equations:

from beamfeat import stability_report

report = stability_report(BeamFeatRegressor(max_depth=2, beam_width=25), X, y, n_splits=30)
print(report)

BeamFeatRegressor refitted on 30 random splits (random_state=0), each fitted on 300 rows and scored on the other 100.

Held-out R^2: mean 1.000, sd 0.000, min 1.000, max 1.000.
1 distinct equation in 30 splits: every split printed it.
1 distinct feature, selected in 30 of the 30 splits.

Equations printed in more than one split, most frequent first:
  30/30  y ~ (x0 * x1)

Features, most frequent first:
  30/30  (x0 * x1)

Features whose values on the rows of X correlate above 0.999 in absolute value are counted as one; an equation is the set of its features, whatever its coefficients.

Every split found the planted product. The diabetes data are another matter:

from sklearn.datasets import load_diabetes

diabetes = load_diabetes(as_frame=True)
report = stability_report(BeamFeatRegressor(), diabetes.data, diabetes.target, n_splits=30)
print(report.summary(max_rows=3))

BeamFeatRegressor refitted on 30 random splits (random_state=0), each fitted on 331 rows and scored on the other 111.

Held-out R^2: mean 0.496, sd 0.050, min 0.389, max 0.575.
30 distinct equations in 30 splits; none recurs.
86 distinct features; the most frequent in 11 of the 30 splits.

Features, most frequent first:
  11/30  ((bmi + s5) + (bp - s3))
   8/30  ((bmi + s5) - (s3 + sex))
   8/30  ((bmi + bp) - (s3 + sex))
  ... and 83 more features

Features whose values on the rows of X correlate above 0.999 in absolute value are counted as one; an equation is the set of its features, whatever its coefficients.

No two of the thirty splits printed the same equation, and their held-out R² ranges from 0.389 to 0.575, a spread that one fit's score would hide. An equation fitted to these data is one draw among many that predict about as well. What recurs is a family of sums and differences of bmi, s5, bp and s3, the commonest member in 11 of the 30 splits. Report that family, with its frequencies, rather than one equation.

Two formulas count as one feature when their values on the rows of X correlate above 0.999 in absolute value. A rewriting such as (x1 - x0) for (x0 - x1) is then not counted twice, and neither is a rescaling or a near-duplicate. An equation is the set of its features, whatever its coefficients. The report keeps everything behind the summary:

  • report.splits[i] has the rows split i was fitted and scored on, its formulas, its equation(), its score and the fitted clone;
  • report.features and report.equations hold the classes, most frequent first, each with the splits it appeared in;
  • report.scores holds the held-out scores.

The splits and the clones' seeds come from random_state (default 0), so a report is reproducible, and n_jobs fits splits in parallel processes without changing it. The regressor is scored by R² and the classifier by accuracy, as their score methods are. A transformer has no score of its own, so it is scored by a ridge regression on its features, or by a logistic regression for classification. When a test row is outside a selected formula's domain, the classifier predicts its most frequent training class there, as its predict does. A regressor or transformer has no score on such a test part, so that split goes unscored, and the summary counts it.

resample chooses what varies. The default, "splits", draws new training and test rows as well as a new seed for every split. It measures split-to-split variability: how far the equation and its score move with another sample of the data. resample="seeds" keeps the first split's rows and varies only the seed, and with it the search/selection split inside each fit. That design, the one in the paper's stability study (Appendix E), measures seed-to-seed variability on fixed data: how much the printed equation owes to one random draw, the draw the FDR guarantee is conditional on. Run on diabetes as above with resample="seeds", it still prints 30 distinct equations in 30 fits, with 84 distinct features and the commonest in 10. The standard deviation of R² falls from 0.050 to 0.008, though, so most of the default's spread comes from the test parts, while the turnover of equations persists with the rows held fixed.

docs.title: LaTeX
docs.text:
latex() typesets equation(): the same terms, coefficients and options (precision, max_terms, style), and the same note when the guarantee covers more terms than are printed. It needs sympy (pip install "beamfeat[display]"), as to_sympy() does.

print(model.latex())
print(model.latex_formulas())

y = 0.9999 x_{0} x_{1} - 0.003943 \quad \text{[1 of 25 certified terms; parsimony=None prints all 25]}
['x_{0} x_{1}']

latex(note=False) leaves the note off, for pasting into a document; the guarantee still covers the screened set, so say so where the equation appears. The string has no math delimiters; wrap it in $...$, or in a notebook use IPython.display.Math(model.latex()). The classifier's latex() gives the log-odds of the positive class, or one softmax score per class in an aligned block, as its equation() does.

docs.title: Export to NumPy, JAX or PyTorch
docs.text:
to_sympy() returns each feature as a sympy expression in real symbols named after the input columns, so sympy.lambdify turns the features into a function for any array library sympy can print to. No extra dependency is involved beyond sympy and the target library:

import sympy

columns = sympy.symbols("x0:4", real=True)  # one symbol per input column, in order
features = sympy.lambdify(columns, model.to_sympy(), modules="numpy")

raw = model.coef_ / model.scaler_.scale_
offset = model.intercept_ - raw @ model.scaler_.mean_
prediction = np.column_stack(features(*X.T)) @ raw + offset  # model.predict(X), to rounding

modules="jax" or modules="torch" (sympy 1.14 or newer) gives the same function on JAX or PyTorch arrays, with jnp.stack(..., axis=1) or torch.stack(..., dim=1) in place of np.column_stack; the coefficients and offset are plain arrays to convert once. Columns of a DataFrame keep their names as symbols when the names are valid identifiers, and are sanitised otherwise; read the symbols from free_symbols of the expressions in that case.

Two differences from transform remain. sympy may rewrite an expression into an equivalent form, so a value can overflow in one and not the other. And a row outside a formula's domain gives whatever the array library gives there, with no warning from beamfeat.

docs.title: Column names flow into formulas
docs.text:
Fit on a DataFrame and formulas use your names:

import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"mass": rng.uniform(1, 5, 300),
                   "vol":  rng.uniform(1, 5, 300)})
target = df["mass"] / df["vol"] + rng.normal(0, 0.02, 300)
print(BeamFeatRegressor(random_state=0).fit(df, target).formulas())

['(mass / vol)']

docs.title: Dimensional analysis
docs.text:
Give units as pint quantities or plain strings; dimensionally invalid expressions (metres plus kilograms) are ruled out before any numerical work — so x0 + x1 (kg plus m) is never even scored:

y_phys = X[:, 0] * X[:, 1] / X[:, 2]          # kg·m/s
model = BeamFeatRegressor(
    units={"x0": "kg", "x1": "m", "x2": "s"}, random_state=0
).fit(X[:, :3], y_phys)
print(model.formulas())

['((x1 / x2) * x0)']

The recovered form, kg·m/s, is exactly the target's dimension — and the dimensionally invalid spellings never consumed a beam slot.

Cover every column. A column without a unit is dimensionally unconstrained, so it combines freely with the labelled ones and the check stops binding on exactly the columns you did not vouch for — labelling your real measurements and leaving the noise blank is the case worth naming, because it looks careful and is not. Give the genuinely unitless columns "dimensionless"; the estimator warns when coverage is partial, and raises when the keys match no column at all. Keys are column names, so a DataFrame lets you write {"rho": "kg/m**3"} rather than {"x0": ...}.

docs.title: Constants inside expressions
docs.text:
The linear model supplies the coefficients outside the expressions. That alone cannot write exp(-x²/2), x^1.5 or (x0 + x1)/(1 + x0·x1), where the constant sits inside a nonlinearity, so the estimators also use operators that carry one fitted constant each, listed in fitted_ops. All four are on by default (since 0.6.0); fitted_ops=() keeps every expression free of constants, as the default did before, and fits about twice as fast on small data. They are a list of their own: restricting unary_ops leaves them on, so unary_ops=() still allows log(x + a) unless fitted_ops=() too.

name expression operand "exp_scaled" exp(a·x) dimensionless "pow" x^a positive, dimensionless "inv_shift" 1/(x + a) any; a takes the operand's unit "log_shift" log(x + a) x + a positive, dimensionless 
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
X = rng.uniform(0.1, 1.0, (500, 2))
y = np.exp(-X[:, 0] ** 2 / 2) + rng.normal(0, 1e-3, 500)
model = BeamFeatRegressor(max_depth=2, random_state=0).fit(X, y)
print(model.formulas(), model.to_sympy())

['exp(-0.5*(x0)^2)'] [exp(-x0**2/2)]

With fitted_ops=() the same data give (x0 + (x0)^2) and log(x0), a surrogate that scores well on this range and says nothing about the law.

How the constants are chosen:

  • Where. At each depth, every listed operator is fitted to every expression in the previous depth's beam (at the first depth, the beam_width best input columns), and to the previous depth's beam_width best candidates that the beam dropped as near-duplicates: two expressions that correlate at 0.95 need not stay alike under 1/(x + a) or exp(a·x). The results join that depth's candidates, to be scored, pruned and kept like any other. The ceiling max_candidates_per_depth counts the operator proposals only.
  • How. Each constant maximises the absolute correlation with the target: a coarse grid scaled to the operand (for exp_scaled, |a| up to 10/max|x|; for pow, a from -4 to 4; for the shifts, poles kept off the observed range), then a golden-section refinement. A fit that runs to the edge of its grid is discarded, and so is one for which the likelihood-ratio test of the snapping step below does not reject the null that the operand on its own fits as well (each operator becomes linear in x at one end of its range). Correlation is used whatever the scorer; the scorer then ranks the result.
  • Poles. inv_shift and log_shift keep their pole away from the data they were fitted on: at least twice the spread of the operand's ten most extreme values at that end, and at least 1% of its range. A pole just past the edge of the data is shaped by the few rows next to it, and the first new row a little further out falls beyond it: NaN for the logarithm, a value of the wrong sign and any size for the reciprocal. A fit that wants its pole closer runs into the bound and is discarded, and snapping never moves a constant past it. The margin widens where the data thin out towards the edge and narrows where they are dense. On 18 real datasets, poles inside it were crossed by a row the fit had not seen in 14% of fits, and poles outside it in 0.3%. A negative power has its pole at 0, so pow fits one only when the operand stays more than the same margin above 0. Otherwise a runs from 0.1 to 4, and a fit that wants less is discarded, since x^a then takes the shape of log(x), which has the same pole.
  • In context. 1/(x0·x1 + a) on its own correlates best with the target as a runs to the pole; only as the denominator of (x0 + x1) is a = 1 identifiable. While the depth limit leaves room, each constant is also fitted as a factor of a beam member, and that product joins the next depth's candidates.
  • Snapping. The constant is replaced by the simplest of 0, ±1, ±2, ±3, ±1/2, ±3/2, ±1/3, ±1/4 for which a likelihood-ratio test at level 0.001 fails to reject the null that the constant takes that value, so exp(-0.49991·x²) is reported as exp(-x²/2). If the test rejects every one of them, the constant is rounded to the fewest significant digits that cost nothing measurable. A snapped constant is exact in to_sympy(), latex() and the printed formulas.
  • Near copies. A fitted constant can also bend an expression into a near copy of a simple law. With 10% noise on log(x0), (x0)^(-0.02) correlates with log(x0) at 0.99999, and since its constant was fitted on the search rows it fits them a little better. So at the end of the search, each kept expression with fitted constants is compared with its near copies among everything the search found (correlation at redundancy_threshold) that carry fewer constants and are not near copies of another kept expression. The snapping test decides, on the same rows: if it fails to reject the null that a copy fits the target as well, the simplest such copy takes the expression's place. Without this step, log(x0), sqrt(x0), 1/x0 and x0² at that noise were printed as themselves in 0, 0, 2 and 2 of 10 fits; with it, in 10, 7, 10 and 8, against 10, 9, 10 and 8 with fitted_ops=(). A law that needs its constant keeps it while the data reject the simpler forms, as the Gaussian and relativistic velocity addition of the physics panel do at 0.1% noise.
  • Stored. The constant is part of the expression: transform, predict and a pickled model reuse it on new data without refitting.

The constants are fitted inside the search, on the search rows only, so the screen on the selection rows sees fixed expressions and its guarantee is unchanged; see the guarantees page.

What it costs. Fitting adds a few candidates per parent and operator, and makes a fit on the Feynman panel about five times slower (about 0.2 s to 1.1 s per equation). Fitted expressions also take beam slots, so enabling them can change what else a depth keeps: within a depth, a constant-free candidate is never dropped as a near-duplicate of a fitted one, but it can be out-ranked, and at the end of the search it takes a fitted expression's place only as described under Near copies. And constants are fitted one at a time, greedily: a law needs its constant-free parts to be among a depth's best candidates first.

docs.title: Columns that carry no data
docs.text:
A column with no variation cannot be selected — it standardises to zeros, so its association with the target is zero wherever it appears. That is the right outcome and costs nothing, but in the output it looks the same as a column that simply does not matter, so it is reported. Real tables have such columns more often than one would think: in the UJIIndoorLoc Wi-Fi fingerprints, dozens of access points never register at all.

stuck = np.full((400, 1), 9.81)               # a sensor stuck at one reading
BeamFeatRegressor(random_state=0).fit(np.hstack([X, stuck]), y)

UserWarning: beamfeat: 1 of 5 columns are constant (x4) and cannot be selected.
They are ignored and cost nothing, but check whether they are meant to carry
data.

Constancy is relative to the column's magnitude, not an absolute floor on the spread — a column varying over 0 to 1e-9 has a smaller variance than a stuck sensor reading 9.81, and only the second is constant. Use is_constant to apply the same test when screening a table before fitting.

A constant with a genuine unit is a different matter: gravity is m/s² whether or not it varies, and expressions built from it are unit-checked, so label it. Its absence from a recovered formula is not a miss — a multiplicative constant is absorbed into the fitted coefficient rather than returned as a symbol.

docs.title: Audit what selection did
docs.text:
Every candidate's permutation p-value and its adjusted q-value is recorded:

for row in model.selection_report_[:3]:
    print(row["formula"], round(row["q_value"], 4), row["kept"])

A feature is kept only if the screen rejects its null at target_fdr (default 0.1, Benjamini–Yekutieli) on the held-out split and the parsimony step then retains it. screened marks the certified set, the candidates whose nulls the screen rejected, which is what the guarantee covers; kept marks the compact subset the equation prints. Set parsimony=None and the two agree.

docs.title: When no null is rejected
docs.text:
On a target with no structure the screen rejects no null, and the model says so instead of returning junk:

noise = rng.standard_normal(400)
model = BeamFeatRegressor(random_state=0).fit(X, noise)
# NoDiscoveriesWarning: ... Returning no constructed features ...
print(model.equation())

y = 0.03527  (no feature selected)

Not on every draw. Under the global null every rejection is a false rejection, so the FDR is the probability that a fit rejects any null at all: up to target_fdr of pure-noise fits still certify features, and when one does, the nulls of correlated candidates tend to be rejected together. The same noise under another search seed can certify a dozen formulas with fdr_controlled_ = True: that is the error the guarantee bounds in expectation, not a breach of it.

Prefer the old behaviour? on_no_discoveries="fallback" keeps the unfiltered search output (flagged fdr_controlled_=False); "raise" raises.

docs.title: Classification
docs.text:
from beamfeat import BeamFeatClassifier

labels = (X[:, 0] * X[:, 1] > X[:, 2] * X[:, 3]).astype(int)
clf = BeamFeatClassifier(max_depth=2, random_state=0).fit(X, labels)
print(clf.equation())          # log-odds form; boundary = zero level set

docs.title: Rows outside a formula's domain
docs.text:
A fitted formula can be undefined on new data that the training data never reached: log(x0) at a negative x0, or 1/(x0) at zero. Such a row is NaN in that formula's column of transform, and predict returns NaN for it; every other row gets exactly the value it would get on its own, whatever else is in the batch. A UserWarning names the formula and counts the rows. The classifier's predict cannot return NaN as a label, so it assigns those rows the most frequent training class, while predict_proba and decision_function return NaN for them, which is how to find them. The regressor's score raises rather than scoring the remaining rows.

Fitted constants do not change this. (x0)^1.5 is NaN for a negative x0, as sqrt(x0) is. A fitted pole keeps a margin from the training rows, but a row far enough outside them can still reach it: (x1)^(-0.5), fitted where x1 lies between 1 and 3, is infinite at x1 = 0, as 1/(x1) would be.

docs.title: Search constraints
docs.text:
max_inputs caps the distinct input columns in one feature: max_inputs=2 admits x0 * log(x0 / x1) but not x0 * x1 / x2. Use it when a feature that mixes many columns would be uninterpretable to you anyway. It is checked as each candidate is constructed, before any numerical work, so a candidate it rules out costs no evaluation and takes no beam slot. search_result_.trace counts them per depth (n_rejected_constraints).

It does not make selection more powerful. The screen's multiple-testing correction runs over the features that reach selection, which the beam already caps at beam_width and max_features however many expressions were proposed; the limit changes which features those are and how long the search takes.

It is off by default (None), and it only ever narrows the search. An expression of depth d combines at most 2^d input columns, so at the default max_depth=2 no feature uses more than four, and max_inputs=4 or more changes nothing; at max_depth=3 the limit matters up to 8. Set it at or above the number of inputs any law you look for needs. A law that needs more cannot be built, and the search returns the best expression within the limit instead:

import numpy as np
from beamfeat import BeamSearch

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
X = rng.uniform(0.5, 3, (400, 8))
y = X[:, 0] * X[:, 1] + X[:, 2] * X[:, 3] + rng.normal(0, 0.1, 400)
for limit in (None, 3):
    search = BeamSearch(max_depth=2, beam_width=30, random_state=0, max_inputs=limit).run(X, y)
    print(limit, search.names[0])

None ((x0 * x1) + (x2 * x3))
3 ((x0 + x2) * sqrt(x1))

On wide data whose signal is spread over many columns, a low limit can still help, because it keeps the beam from filling with combinations of many columns. Compare the held-out score with and without it rather than assuming either way.

docs.title: Laws whose parts the score cannot see
docs.text:
The search keeps, at each depth, the candidates that correlate best with the target and builds the next depth from them. A law can need a part that does not correlate with the target at all. With inputs centred on zero, x0 and x1 are each uncorrelated with x0*x1, and every pairwise product is uncorrelated with x0*x1*x2: the score ranks those parts among the noise, and the beam drops them before they can be combined. On positive inputs, as in most physical tables, each factor of a product correlates with it, and the problem does not arise.

benchmarks/search_stress/ measures what it costs. At the defaults, with 500 rows and 10% noise, the search recovered x0*x1*x2 on centred uniform inputs in 54% of fits with 20 columns, 18% with 100 and 10% with 300, and in every fit on positive inputs; each miss was the first depth's beam dropping the pairwise products. A beam of 200 lifted the 20-column figure to 96% at about nine times the fit time, but the 100-column one only to 26%. Past the proposal ceiling, from about 258 columns at the defaults, a centred pair can be lost before it is scored: with 1,000 columns x0*x1 was recovered in 32% of fits, because neither input scored well enough for the pair to be proposed. A miss mostly ends in no equation and a NoDiscoveriesWarning, sometimes in terms that ride on one of the law's columns.

magnitude_slots adds beam slots for candidates whose magnitude tracks the target's:

rng = np.random.default_rng(3)
X = rng.uniform(-1, 1, (400, 10))
y = X[:, 0] * X[:, 1] * X[:, 2] + rng.normal(0, 0.01, 400)
for slots in (0, 3):
    model = BeamFeatRegressor(max_depth=2, beam_width=10, magnitude_slots=slots).fit(X, y)
    print(slots, model.formulas())

0 []
3 ['(x0 * (x1 * x2))']

The first fit finds nothing and warns NoDiscoveriesWarning.

How it works:

  • The score. A candidate c is scored by the absolute correlation of log(1 + |c|/rms(c)) with the same transform of the centred target, where rms is the root mean square. The logarithm turns a product into a sum, so a factor's magnitude tracks the product's even where the factor itself does not correlate with it. The 1 keeps the rows where a product nears zero, and the noise there, from dominating, and it compresses a heavy tail, so that a ratio with a denominator near zero does not score by accident. On more than 1,000 search rows the score is computed on 1,000 of them, evenly spaced, which is plenty to rank a few slots and keeps its cost from growing with the table.
  • The slots. After the beam_width candidates the score keeps, up to magnitude_slots more are kept from the rest, best magnitude score first, under the same redundancy check. They are kept at every depth but the last, since they are there to be built on.
  • The proposals. When the first depth cannot propose every pair of inputs, the inputs are proposed in an order that interleaves their magnitude ranking with their score ranking. The magnitude ranking takes the first place and magnitude_slots / (beam_width + magnitude_slots) of those after it.
  • A part behind a visible term. In x0*x1 + x2 the product does correlate with the target, but hundreds of sums of x2 with another column can outrank it. The search then relies on scoring candidates against the residual left by the inputs, and with more inputs than search rows that residual is empty. The magnitude score is also taken against the residual on the best-scoring columns, at most a quarter as many as the rows, which keeps x0*x1 in view.

Measured at 10 slots on the stress test, it recovered x0*x1*x2 on centred inputs in every fit with 20, 100 and 300 columns, the centred pair in every fit with 1,000 columns, and x0*x1 + x2 with 300 columns and 250 search rows in 88% of fits, where the default recovered none; in no setting did it lose a law the default found. Fits took 1.2 to 1.7 times as long there, and 1.4 times on the high-dimensional study's three 10,000-row tables. Where no such law is hidden it changes little either way: the main suite's mean held-out score over 24 regression datasets went from 0.885 to 0.884, with diabetes and california housing about 0.01 lower, and the high-dimensional study's mean from 0.647 to 0.649. Try it when a law may hide behind centred or signed inputs, and keep it if the held-out score agrees.

It is for regression only, since a class label has no magnitude to track. The ranking runs inside the search, on the search rows only, so the screen on the selection rows sees fixed expressions and its guarantee is unchanged; see the guarantees page. It was measured on products and on a product beside a visible term, and a law whose parts the magnitude score cannot see either is still out of reach.

docs.title: Real data with missing values or categoricals
docs.text:
beamfeat never imputes or encodes silently — compose explicitly:

from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer

pipe = make_pipeline(SimpleImputer(strategy="median"),
                     BeamFeatRegressor(random_state=0))

docs.title: Predicting with the original columns as well
docs.text:
The regressor predicts from the certified features alone, so the fitted model is the equation it prints. When accuracy matters more than a readable model, fit the final model on the original columns plus the certified features:

from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer
from sklearn.linear_model import RidgeCV
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline, make_union
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

from beamfeat import BeamFeatTransformer

model = make_pipeline(
    make_union("passthrough", BeamFeatTransformer(random_state=0)),
    SimpleImputer(strategy="median"),  # rows outside a formula's domain
    StandardScaler(),
    RidgeCV(),
).fit(X, y)

This helps when the signal is spread thinly over many columns, which a few certified features cannot capture but a penalised fit on every column can, and when the certified features add structure a linear model on the raw columns misses. Two things change:

  • The model is no longer interpretable. It has a coefficient for every input column, so it reads like ridge regression, not like an equation.
  • The guarantee is unchanged but narrower in scope. The FDR guarantee covers which constructed features are reported, and those are the same as without the original columns. It says nothing about the coefficients the final model puts on the raw columns.

If the combined model scores no better than ridge on the original columns alone, the certified features are adding nothing to prediction on that data.

docs.title: Speed and memory on wide data
docs.text:
n_jobs spreads the search over cores, and -1 uses all of them. The workers are threads, since numpy releases the GIL while it scores, or processes for the gradient-boosting scorer, whose model fits do not. Apart from that scorer, a depth with fewer than 4096 candidates is scored in the calling thread, so the setting pays off on wide tables rather than on a handful of columns. It never changes the fit: features, p-values and predictions are identical for every value.

model = BeamFeatRegressor(random_state=0, n_jobs=-1).fit(X, y)

Memory does not grow with the number of candidates either. Each depth is evaluated and scored in chunks of about 8 MiB and only the scores are kept, so a default fit on 1000 columns and 600 rows peaks at about 0.35 GB. BeamSearch(chunk_size=...) sets the chunk size directly, again without changing the result. The exceptions are mutual information, which draws its noise for a whole depth, and a custom scorer that does not declare itself separable: both still receive a depth at once.

docs.title: When to reach for something else
docs.text: If a tree model beats beamfeat by a wide margin, your signal is likely piecewise, not algebraic — use the tree. fitted_ops covers one constant per operator, fitted one operator at a time; if your law needs several constants fitted jointly (exp(-a·x)·cos(b·x + c)), constants inside sums or products (a·x0 + b·x1 under a logarithm), or deeper nesting than the beam reaches, use a symbolic regressor such as PySR. The guarantees page states every boundary with the measurement behind it.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text: Three levels, depending on what you need. Most people only need the first.

docs.title: Use the library
docs.text:
pip install beamfeat              # numpy, scikit-learn, joblib
pip install "beamfeat[units]"     # + pint, for dimensional analysis
pip install "beamfeat[display]"   # + sympy, for to_sympy() and latex()
pip install "beamfeat[all]"       # + both, pandas and the test dependencies

Python 3.10 or newer. There are no upper version pins. The test suite is run against the newest releases on Python 3.10 to 3.15, where all 965 tests pass (scikit-learn 1.9.1 from Python 3.11, and 1.7.2, the newest that supports it, on 3.10; numpy 2.2 to 2.5), and against the oldest supported stack (scikit-learn 1.6.1, numpy 1.26, joblib 1.2), which leaves pint and pandas out so that the tests that need them show they skip cleanly without them. CI repeats this every week, and runs the suite against the upcoming releases of numpy, SciPy, scikit-learn and pandas too, so that a breaking change upstream is seen before it ships.

Nothing below is needed to use beamfeat.

cd beamfeat
