docs.title: Migrating from autofeat
docs.text:
Examined against autofeat 2.1.3, the current release as of July 2026, in the pinned comparison environment (scikit-learn 1.7.2); the version-compatibility failures below were reproduced on scikit-learn 1.8 and 1.9.

beamfeat's design began from a review of autofeat (Horn et al., 2019) and keeps its central idea — compact symbolic features feeding a linear model. The APIs are close enough that most code ports in a few lines. This page is a reference for doing so; it is not a claim that one tool supersedes the other, and autofeat's exhaustive expansion still finds structure a beam search prunes (see the Where autofeat does better section below).

docs.title: Version compatibility
docs.text:
If you arrived here from an error, this is likely the one:

TypeError: check_array() got an unexpected keyword argument 'force_all_finite'

autofeat 2.1.3 raises this when transforming or predicting on unseen data after engineering at least one feature, on scikit-learn ≥ 1.8 — the argument was renamed ensure_all_finite in 1.6 and removed in 1.8. fit still succeeds, so the failure appears only when you apply the fitted model to a test set. Its declared pins (numpy<2.0, pandas<3.0) will also downgrade a current environment on installation.

beamfeat declares no upper version bounds and its test suite runs unpatched from scikit-learn 1.6 through 1.9.

docs.title: Worked example
docs.text:
# autofeat
from autofeat import AutoFeatRegressor
model = AutoFeatRegressor(feateng_steps=2, featsel_runs=5, verbose=0)
model.fit(X_train, y_train)
print(model.new_feat_cols_)
predictions = model.predict(X_test)

# beamfeat
from beamfeat import BeamFeatRegressor
model = BeamFeatRegressor(max_depth=2, target_fdr=0.1, random_state=0)
model.fit(X_train, y_train)
print(model.formulas())
print(model.equation())          # the fitted model, readable
print(model.fdr_controlled_)     # check before treating features as vetted
predictions = model.predict(X_test)

docs.title: Where autofeat does better
docs.text: Exhaustive expansion does not need to see a signal marginally in order to generate the right basis. On targets with a strong non-monotone interaction — Friedman #1 is the standard example — autofeat's brute-force expansion finds structure that correlation-guided beam search prunes. On four of five splits of Friedman #1 it reaches R² 0.94 to 0.96 where beamfeat reaches 0.72 to 0.79; on the fifth it returns −103. Take the win on the typical split as real and the mean as unusable, which is the shape of the trade: beamfeat accepts a lower ceiling as the price of a guarantee and a floor. Quantified in Statistical guarantees.

docs.title: Behavioural differences to expect
docs.text:
• Fewer features. Selection is a multiple hypothesis test rather than a noise-threshold heuristic: a feature is selected when the test rejects its null, and a parsimony step then retains a compact subset of the selected features. Expect single-digit feature counts where autofeat returns tens. equation() records how many of the certified terms it printed, and parsimony=None returns the whole certified set if you want it.
  • A guarantee, and an honest empty result. If the screen rejects no null, beamfeat returns no constructed features, warns, and sets fdr_controlled_ = False rather than returning unvetted candidates. Check that flag.
  • Determinism. random_state makes the whole pipeline reproducible, whatever n_jobs is set to. autofeat exposes none, and cannot be made reproducible from outside: its noise-injection screen draws decoy features from the global NumPy generator before its own internal seeding applies, so each process starts from different entropy. Six runs of one identical split returned R² from +0.952 to −109.8.
  • Constants inside expressions. autofeat fits none. Since 0.6.0 beamfeat fits one constant inside an expression by default, such as exp(-3.2 x) or 1/(x + a) (fitted_ops; fitted_ops=() turns it off). If a law needs several constants fitted jointly, a symbolic regressor such as PySR is the right instrument.

docs.title: Getting started with beamfeat¶
docs.text:
beamfeat constructs interpretable features from tabular data. Given columns a, b, and c, it searches expressions like log(a), a * b, and (a * b) / c, tests each against the null hypothesis that it is independent of the target, and reports the ones whose null is rejected as readable formulas.

Two things distinguish it from exhaustive feature engineering:

  1. The search is guided. Candidates are scored against the target and only the best are extended, so cost does not compound with expression depth.
  2. Selection is calibrated. A feature is retained only when a test rejects its null under false-discovery-rate control, not when it clears a heuristic threshold.

This notebook covers the basic workflow. Later notebooks cover the search and selection machinery in detail.

docs.title: A problem with a known answer¶
docs.text: We generate data where the target is a known function of the inputs, so we can check whether beamfeat recovers it. The relationship is y = (a * b) / c, which no linear model on the raw columns can represent.

docs.title: Fitting¶
docs.text: BeamFeatRegressor follows the usual scikit-learn interface. The two parameters that matter most are max_depth, which bounds expression complexity, and beam_width, which bounds how many expressions survive each depth.

docs.title: Watching it work¶
docs.text: verbose is a level. 0 is silent, 1 prints a line per stage, and 2 adds per-depth search detail and the strongest certified candidates with their p- and q-values. It is the quickest way to see where a fit spent its effort, and to tell a search that found nothing from a screen that rejected no null.

docs.title: Reading what it found¶
docs.text: This is the part a gradient-boosted model cannot give you. The fitted model exposes both the individual feature formulas and the full equation.

docs.title: Comparing against a linear baseline¶
docs.text: The point of constructing features is to let a simple model fit a relationship it otherwise could not.

docs.title: Using it in a pipeline¶
docs.text: BeamFeatTransformer constructs features without fitting a model, so it composes with any downstream estimator. Because construction happens inside fit, cross-validating the pipeline does not leak information across folds.

docs.title: Classification¶
docs.text: BeamFeatClassifier works the same way, with predict_proba and decision_function available as usual.

docs.title: Search and scoring¶
docs.text:
This notebook covers how beamfeat explores the space of expressions, and how the choice of scorer changes what it finds.

The core problem is that expression space is enormous. With 5 input columns, 5 unary operators, and 4 binary operators, exhaustive expansion to depth 3 produces well over a million candidates, and each must be evaluated before it can be judged. Beam search avoids this by scoring candidates as they are generated and extending only the most promising.

docs.title: Running a search directly¶
docs.text: BeamSearch is the layer beneath the estimators. Using it directly is useful when you want to inspect the search rather than fit a model.

docs.title: The trace¶
docs.text: Every search records what happened at each depth. This is how you attribute cost, and how you notice a beam that collapsed or saturated.

docs.title: How beam width controls cost¶
docs.text: Beam width is the parameter that bounds work. Widening it explores more of the space at a cost that grows faster than the width, since each expression in the beam is combined with every expression kept so far; narrowing it risks pruning a parent whose children would have been valuable.

docs.title: How depth controls expressiveness¶
docs.text: Some relationships simply cannot be expressed below a certain depth. (a * b) / c needs depth 2: one step to build a * b, another to divide by c.

docs.title: Workers and memory¶
docs.text:
At the defaults a depth may propose up to 200,000 candidates (max_candidates_per_depth), so the search evaluates and scores a depth in chunks and keeps only the scores; the candidates the redundancy check reaches, usually a small share of the round, are evaluated again. Memory stays bounded however many candidates a depth proposes. chunk_size sets how many candidates make a chunk, by default as many as fit in 8 MiB. Mutual information is the exception: it draws its noise for the whole batch, so it still scores a depth at once.

n_jobs spreads the chunks over joblib workers: threads, since numpy releases the GIL, or processes for gradient boosting, whose model fits hold it. -1 uses every core. A depth of fewer than 4096 candidates stays in the calling thread unless the scorer fits models, since starting workers would cost more than it saves, so on the four-column problem above n_jobs changes nothing. The estimators take the same argument.

Neither setting changes the result, for the scorers that draw random numbers too: no seed depends on a worker or a chunk. On forty columns, where both depths are large enough for workers:

docs.title: Choosing a scorer¶
docs.text:
Four scoring strategies are available, and they differ in what they can detect and what they cost.

  • "correlation" — absolute Pearson correlation against the residual. One dot product per candidate. The default.
  • "spearman" — absolute rank correlation against the same residual, for a sort per column more. Sees any monotone relationship and is insensitive to outlying values.
  • "mutual_information" — nearest-neighbour mutual information. Detects dependence that correlation misses.
  • "gradient_boosting" — measured out-of-fold predictive improvement. Scores what is actually being optimised.

docs.title: Where they agree¶
docs.text: On a relationship whose nonlinearity is captured by the expression itself, the first three find the same thing, and correlation is much the cheapest. Gradient boosting is left out: it fits models for every candidate, which on a round of this size takes far longer still.

docs.title: Where they differ¶
docs.text: Correlation is blind to symmetric relationships. If the target depends on the magnitude of a feature but not its sign, correlation sees nothing while mutual information sees the dependence clearly.

docs.title: Redundancy control¶
docs.text: A beam scored purely on individual merit fills with variants of the same signal. beamfeat scores each candidate against the residual left by what the beam already holds as well as against the target, and ranks it on the larger of the two, so a refinement of a beam member survives while novelty is still rewarded. It also drops a candidate too correlated with one already admitted at the same depth; the final ranking applies the same check across depths.

docs.title: Auditing what the search ruled out¶
docs.text: Candidates excluded during evaluation are recorded rather than silently dropped. This matters when a search returns less than expected: the log tells you whether candidates were numerically invalid, degenerate, copies of a column already there — abs of a column that is never negative is the column itself — or simply never proposed.

def gaussian_design(seed, n=300, n_signal=5, n_noise=20, effect=3.0):
    trial_rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    n_features = n_signal + n_noise
    features = trial_rng.standard_normal((n, n_features))
    coefficients = np.zeros(n_features)
    coefficients[:n_signal] = effect
    target = features @ coefficients + trial_rng.standard_normal(n)
    truth = np.zeros(n_features, dtype=bool)
    truth[:n_signal] = True
    return features, target, truth


def realised_fdr(selector_factory, nominal, n_trials=15):
    false_rates, recalls = [], []
    for trial in range(n_trials):
        features, target, truth = gaussian_design(3000 + trial)
        result = selector_factory(nominal, trial).select(features, target)
        if result.n_selected:
            false_rates.append(np.sum(~truth[result.selected]) / result.n_selected)
        else:
            false_rates.append(0.0)
        recalls.append(np.sum(truth[result.selected]) / truth.sum())
    return np.mean(false_rates), np.mean(recalls)

docs.title: Selection and units¶
docs.text:
Feature construction proposes far more candidates than any dataset can support. Selection decides which of them are reported, and it is where most automated feature engineering tools are weakest: an importance threshold gives no guarantee about how many reported features are noise, and the expected number of false discoveries grows with the size of the candidate pool.

beamfeat tests each candidate against its own null hypothesis, that the candidate is independent of the target, and selects the candidates whose nulls it rejects. It controls the false discovery rate — the expected proportion of rejected nulls that are true, that is, of selected features that are spurious.

docs.title: The problem, demonstrated¶
docs.text: With a pure-noise target every null is true, so every rejection is a false rejection. A well-calibrated selector should reject almost nothing.

docs.title: Measured calibration¶
docs.text: More usefully: with real signal present, what fraction of the rejections are false? This is the quantity the library claims to control.

docs.title: Knockoffs: two constructions, two sets of assumptions¶
docs.text:
The knockoff filter comes in two forms, and it matters which one you mean.

Fixed-X knockoffs (Barber & Candès, 2015) treat the design as fixed and make no assumption about the distribution of the features — deterministic engineered columns are admissible. The guarantee needs n > 2p and Gaussian noise in y = Xβ + ε. Engineered designs strain it in two ways. Near-duplicate columns drive the construction's s toward zero, the knockoffs become nearly identical to the originals, and the filter loses the ability to tell them apart: a cost in power, not validity. Exact dependence is worse. When the design covariance has an eigenvalue below 1e-6 — a constant column, or one that is a linear combination of others, as a + b is of a and b — the knockoffs of the columns involved can only equal the originals, the lasso's tie-breaking then favours the originals, and that costs validity. beamfeat leaves such columns out of the construction, so they cannot be selected, and names them in its warning.

Model-X knockoffs (Candès et al., 2018) instead assume the features are jointly Gaussian — which engineered features are not: log(a) and a * b are deterministic functions of shared parents. beamfeat only uses this construction when n <= 2p, where the fixed-X construction does not exist, and warns.

beamfeat routes between the two automatically and reports which assumptions are under strain, rather than pretending otherwise.

One thing knockoffs will not do, since the conditional null invites the inference: they cannot prune a term out of an expression. Selection operates on whole candidate columns, so a candidate like noise + (a * b) / c is one column with one null, rejected or not as a whole — switching the selector does not reach inside it. Two levers do: constraining what gets built, which notebook 04 does with units, and testing each column inside a candidate, which the estimators' input_test=True does.

docs.title: End to end¶
docs.text: Putting search and selection together: construct candidates, then keep only those whose nulls the FDR-controlled test rejects.

docs.title: Dimensional analysis¶
docs.text:
If your columns carry physical units, supplying them restricts the search to dimensionally valid expressions. Adding a mass to a length is ruled out at construction time, before any numerical work happens.

This is both a correctness feature and a performance one: it prunes large parts of the search space for free.

docs.title: Units through the estimator API¶
docs.text: The same constraint is available on the estimators via the units argument. The fitted equation is compact because, after FDR screening, the estimator keeps a parsimonious forward-selected subset of the screened features by default (parsimony="forward"); the equation's suffix records how many of the certified terms it printed, and the full screened set with per-candidate p- and q-values is available in selection_report_.

The same over-deep search now returns the clean core. Identical R^2, no parasites — and the effect is not just in the pruned equation: across the whole certified set, not one formula adds a noise column to a dimensioned quantity, against almost all of them before. That is the general lesson — where a statistical criterion cannot separate two candidates, a structural constraint often can, and it costs nothing because it applies before any numerical work.

Two cautions about what units check.

They enforce that an expression is internally coherent, not that it matches the target's dimension. rho * Q * H / eta is kg·m/s while power is watts, and nothing objects, because g was absorbed. Units rule out nonsense; they will not tell you a factor is missing.

And a dimensionless column is legal almost everywhere. Q / noise_7 is still m³/s, so noise can ride in multiplicatively even under a full labelling, and most of the certified set still mentions one. What units removed is the whole class of violations — adding a bare number to a physical quantity — not every appearance of an irrelevant column.

The gap matters. Parsimony picks a subset by greedy forward selection on the same rows, and a data-dependent subset of an FDR-controlled set does not inherit the guarantee: pruning cannot add false discoveries, but it can raise the false discovery proportion, because the denominator shrinks faster than the numerator, and fdp_inflation_ reports by how much. What that costs in fit is small and has been measured — about a thousandth of R^2 across 308 paired fits, held out in every study but one scored in-sample, in benchmarks/PARSIMONY_COST.md. Report the screened set when you need the guarantee; use the equation when you need something to read.

Lines 2 to 4 each add a term that pairs part of the core with a noise column and gains less than 1e-4 of R^2 — the noisy members of the fifty certified formulas, met one at a time, and the reason the forward step stopped after line 1. Complexity counts the nodes of each term's expression tree, plus one per term for its coefficient. The R^2 is in-sample, on the rows screening used, and the lines carry no coefficients because only the marked one has been fitted.

The last line of the output is the one to keep in mind. Every line is a subset of the screened set chosen on the rows screening used, so picking line 3 because it reads well is the same kind of choice the forward step makes, and the guarantee covers it no more than it covers line 1. It covers line 50, the screened set itself, which is the equation parsimony=None fits. The records behind the text are in equations_.

An intercept-only model and a visible warning, which is the correct answer: there was nothing to find, and the constructor declined to invent it. fdr_controlled_ reads False here rather than True — no feature was returned, so nothing carries the guarantee, and the flag describes what came back rather than how hard the procedure tried.

The other case looks identical from the outside but is not. If the candidate pool is large enough that the multiplicity threshold falls below the smallest p-value the permutation budget can produce, the correction cannot reject anything, whatever the data say. The selector detects this and says so in its warning, naming the correction and what to change. So read the warning before concluding there is no signal: an empty selection with a budget warning means that no null could have been rejected at that budget, not that the data are silent.

The column names are valid identifiers, so the symbols carry them unchanged; other names are sanitised, and the expressions' free_symbols show what they became.

Two differences from predict remain. sympy may rewrite an expression into an equivalent form — (H / eta) * (Q * rho) came back as H*Q*rho/eta — so a value can overflow in one and not the other. And a row outside a formula's domain gives whatever the array library gives there, where predict gives NaN and a warning.

docs.title: Reading a fit¶
docs.text:
The three notebooks before this one plant an answer and check that beamfeat finds it. Real fits do not arrive that way. They arrive as an equation you did not write, containing columns you did not expect, with fdr_controlled_ reporting True and no obvious way to tell a triumph from a coincidence.

This notebook is about that moment. We take a problem with a known physical answer, hide it among noise, and then get it wrong on purpose — because the ways it goes wrong are more instructive than the way it goes right, and every one of them has a fix.

docs.title: The problem¶
docs.text:
Hydraulic power of a centrifugal pump, P = rho * g * Q * H / eta: density, gravity, flow rate, head, efficiency. Five real variables, buried among eight columns of plausible-looking nonsense — the ambient noise any plant historian is full of.

Note that g is a constant. Keep an eye on it.

docs.title: Start at the defaults¶
docs.text: Always. The defaults are max_depth=2, beam_width=50.

docs.title: Where did gravity go?¶
docs.text:
It is in the coefficient. g never varies, so no expression containing it can be distinguished from the same expression without it: rho * g is just 9.81 * rho, perfectly collinear with rho, and the redundancy pass keeps one representative of the pair. The scaling then lands in the linear model, which is why the fitted coefficient reads 9.80 rather than 1. Under parsimony=None the same scaling is shared across fifty collinear terms and the leading coefficient reads lower, which is why a constant is easiest to read off the compact fit.

This generalises. A multiplicative constant is absorbed into the coefficient rather than recovered as a symbol, so its absence from the formula is not a miss. Check the coefficient before concluding a factor was lost.

docs.title: Searching harder makes it worse¶
docs.text: Five variables feels like it should need a deep search. Let us give it one: depth 3, and a wider beam. verbose=1 shows what each stage did.

docs.title: Why the flag is still True¶
docs.text:
This is the single most important thing to understand about the guarantee, and it is not a defect.

The null being tested is marginal: is this expression, as a whole, independent of the target? An expression that combines the true core with a noise column is emphatically not independent of the target — the core sees to that — so its null is false and rejecting it is not an error under the criterion. The guarantee bounds the expected share of selected formulas that are pure noise. It says nothing about whether every column inside a formula earns its place.

So fdr_controlled_ = True means what it says, and it is not the property you wanted here. Noise hitchhikes on a strong signal.

docs.title: Depth is not the number of variables¶
docs.text:
The instinct that sent us to max_depth=3 was wrong arithmetic. Depth counts composition levels, not variables, and a binary operator combines any two surviving expressions — not a variable onto a chain.

So rho * Q * H / eta, four variables, is depth two:

depth built 1 (Q * H) and (eta / rho) 2 (Q * H) / (eta / rho)

The default reached it on the first try. The extra level bought no accuracy and gave the search room to decorate a finished answer with noise. Raise max_depth when a target you expect is not being recovered, never speculatively: a deeper search enlarges the candidate pool, every threshold scales as 1/m, and each extra candidate costs power on the ones that matter.

docs.title: Units are the fix¶
docs.text: The screen cannot tell that noise_0 does not belong — as we just saw, the expression is genuinely associated with the target once noise_0 is attached to the core. Physics can. You cannot add a dimensionless number to a quantity in kg·m/s, and beamfeat rules out such expressions at construction, before they are ever scored. (There is a statistical route too: input_test=True tests each column inside each term, as the guide describes.)

docs.title: Cover every column¶
docs.text: Labelling the five real measurements and leaving the noise columns blank looks like the careful thing to do. It is not.

docs.title: The equation is not the certified set¶
docs.text: equation() prints the parsimony subset, and its suffix says so. The guarantee covers the larger screened set, which selection_report_ holds in full, with a permutation p-value and its q-value per candidate.

docs.title: The equation at every size¶
docs.text: The forward step adds terms one at a time and stops when the next would add less than parsimony_tol to R^2. equations() continues it through the whole screened set, one equation per number of terms, so you can see what the stopping point traded away. On the default fit from the start:

docs.text: Two very different situations produce an empty selection, and they have different fixes. Here is the honest one — a target that is pure noise.

docs.title: Running it elsewhere¶
docs.text: to_sympy() returns each feature as a sympy expression in real symbols named after the columns, so sympy.lambdify turns the features into a function of plain arrays. Fold the model's standardisation into its coefficients and that reproduces predict:

docs.title: A checklist¶
docs.text:
• Start at the defaults. Raise beam_width when an expected target is missed; raise max_depth only when the target genuinely needs the depth, and count composition levels, not variables.
  • An equation that grew noise terms is a sign you searched too deep, not that you need to search deeper.
  • fdr_controlled_ = True says the guarantee holds: on average at most target_fdr of the certified formulas are noise. It does not say every column in a formula belongs; input_test=True tests that.
  • Supply units when you have them, for every column.
  • A missing constant is usually in the coefficient.
  • Quote selection_report_ when you need the guarantee; quote equation() when you need a sentence.
  • An equation picked from equations() carries no more of the guarantee than equation() does, and latex(note=False) drops the note, not the caveat.
  • Read the warnings. They distinguish states that look identical from outside.
